tweets.text:
Nvidia’s $500B financing platforms, CME’s announcement of compute futures referencing Silicon Data indices, and our Series A all landed within days of each other. The timing is revealing.

As the industry moves from the training era into the inference era, compute is becoming a core production input. Post-trained open models, surging inference demand, and deeper enterprise adoption are arriving together. Inference compute is also becoming more fungible.

AI scaling is increasingly a capital problem rather than a pure technology problem: how the buildout gets financed, and who bears which risks. These are questions traditional capital markets are well equipped to answer, especially as inference income stabilizes and data centers begin to resemble more conventional capital assets.

These cash-settled futures give providers and buyers tools to manage that cost volatility the same way oil and crop futures helped those industries plan and expand with greater confidence. They are only the beginning. Rising fungibility will eventually open the door to physically settled instruments as well.

(Note: earlier company post incorrectly listed @CMEGroup instead of @CMEVentures as an investor. Funding is still secured. 😊)

tweets.text:
Eric's message to SaaS CEOs navigating the shift to AI. 

Every day you hit your pre-AI plan, you're destroying value:

"One of the big messages to these SaaS companies a few years ago was, get to AI or be worth 3x revenue. Those are your choices.

Our whole careers we learned you lay out a plan, you execute against it relentlessly and violently and that's how you build equity value. 

That's what these CEOs learned pre-AI. 

Now, every day you hit that plan, you're destroying value.

Another articulation of this is from my friend @anneleeskates. The CEOs who were going through this transitory period and had a business that was at hundreds of millions and they thought that they're all ready. 

They were working on their business from 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM and then trying to do AI from 5:00 to 8:00 in the evenings. 

What they needed to be doing was the inverse."

#Uranium #Copper #Silver #Gold #CPI

CPI is the biggest market catalyst today.

At 8:30 ET / 14:30 Sweden, we get July U.S. inflation, and this could set the direction for metals into the next leg.

Consensus is roughly:
• Headline CPI: +0.1% MoM / +3.4% YoY
• Core CPI: +0.2% MoM / +2.5% YoY

The roadmap is simple:

🔥 Hot CPI → higher yields + stronger dollar → likely initial pressure on gold, silver and copper.

✅ In line → inflation continues cooling → probably supportive for metals, with the broader bull trends intact.

🚀 Cool CPI → lower yields + weaker dollar + less Fed tightening risk → potentially explosive for gold and silver, while copper and uranium equities could benefit from stronger risk appetite and easier financial conditions.

#Silver #Uranium #Copper #Graphene #AI $NVDA

AI may be a technology revolution.

But physically, it’s also a massive infrastructure buildout.

And that means metals, cooling and power on an enormous scale.

$NVDA just announced plans with some of the world’s biggest pools of capital to mobilize $500B+ for AI infrastructure.

That means a LOT more than chips.

🥈 SILVER
At ~350,000 oz/GW, a hypothetical 77 GW buildout could use around 27 Moz of silver.

That’s roughly 40% of the projected 2026 silver deficit.

And silver is already heading for its 6th straight market deficit.

🟠 COPPER
AI data centers can require around 30–47 tonnes of copper per MW.

77 GW could mean roughly 2.3–3.6 MILLION tonnes of copper.

That’s equivalent to around 10–16% of one year’s global mine supply.

And copper was already tight BEFORE AI really took off.

☢️ URANIUM
Then comes the power.

AI needs reliable electricity 24/7.

Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Meta are already turning to nuclear.

If nuclear supplied just 20% of that hypothetical 77 GW buildout, it could mean around 6M lbs of extra U3O8 demand every year.

In a market where reactor demand already exceeds primary mine supply.

⚫ GRAPHENE
And AI has another huge problem:

HEAT.

HydroGraph $HG / $HGRAF is already targeting data centers with its turbostratic fractal graphene, including potential uses in liquid cooling, thermal management, ESD flooring and concrete.

👇 My top #Silver, #Uranium, #Copper and #Graphene picks below

baseline fact: 

- the median Loudoun homeowner owns a home worth $800k and they pay on average $2.7k less in property taxes because of data centers (you can easily compare against neighboring counties for proof). 

- the average residential ratepayer in VA paid 16c/kwh in 2026, up from 11.3c/kwh a decade prior. this increase is mostly due to inflation, not datacenters. 

a typical  Loudoun homeowner will pay $2053 in electricity this year up from $1408 a decade ago. about $138 of that increase is due to datacenters (according to PJM, that keeps a close record of this stuff). 

so they're paying ~$600/year more in power (most of which is due to inflation), around $138/year of that is due to datacenters, but datacenters are also giving them a property tax dividend of $2.7k a year, so they are coming out +$2000/year ahead on average. 

different math for renters, but the baseline facts are the same

Impressive work!

For comparison, an H100 can do roughly 100-200 tok/s of Muse 30B for raw inference single-thread, going up to low thousands of tok/s with a large number of threads - and I am sure that for the massively-multi-threaded case they can optimize the prover further.

So we roughly, sort of, have single-digit (<10x) overhead for LLM proving!

Next step is getting single-digit overheads for FHE, and then ultimately vFHE (aka STARK * FHE). A crazy ambitious milestone given present FHE overheads, but because of how highly structured and almost-linear LLM inference is, it's closer to the realm of possibility than you might think.

Single-digit-overhead all the things.
 https://t.co/NXOTrPTjp6

tweets.text:
Nobody is ready for this number

the median American worker has $955 saved for retirement

not 955k. 955 dollars…

When it comes to this conversation people tend to quote the average. But a handful of rich savers drag the average up and hide the fact that the guy in the middle has basically nothing.

and here's what drives me mad... everyone calls this a discipline problem. "should've saved more"

But you cannot save your way out of this

The whole plan was: earn a wage, buy assets and hold for 40 years. It worked when wages kept up with assets. they don't anymore. wages have lost HALF their purchasing power vs the S&P since 2008

So you're told to buy the one thing that runs away from your paycheck faster every year

Even people who did everything right are still screwed. It's not them. it's the plan.

I wrote out my thoughts on this in full today I’ll link the piece below.

The aim, every business cycle, is to build more intelligence... more GDP.

1. Population is the raw compute, the nodes in the network.
2. Productivity is the intelligence each of those nodes generates.
3. Debt is the energy you pump in when the first two stop carrying the load.

When the first two are firing, the economy compounds. When they stall, debt takes over, and the debasement that follows is what holds the whole thing together. That's most of the developed world since 2008.

In a debasing economy capital flows almost entirely to two places... technology and crypto. They're the only things that still scale economic intelligence, so they compound faster than everything around them.

@RealVision

$INTC - Summary of the podcast for $INTC Bulls:

- CEO alignment is the core asset. Turned Cadence from ~$2.42 to a ~3,000% return over 15 years. He stays 10-15 years, told the Intel board explicitly he's not a short-term guy, and took the job at an age where he could retire instead.

- Demand pull is real and current. He says CEOs are calling him daily asking for more CPU — agentic AI and inference driving it. That's a revenue-line statement, not a vision statement.

- Vertical integration as the differentiator. Product + advanced packaging + foundry bundled together is his claimed value creation. Intel is the only US firm at leading edge scale — Washington, Nvidia and SoftBank on the cap table.

- Fixing the CPU franchise directly. Admits Intel lost the CPU lead and made "a lot of mistakes" in server. Actively recruiting top CPU, GPU, system and software architects for a full stack — targeting agentic AI, edge, and physical AI, not just PC client.

- Packaging is the option value. EMIB, glass substrates, artificial diamond insulators, microfluidic cooling. He funds startups in these areas personally, then spins them in or acquires them.

- Memory optionality. Hired the ex-SK Hynix head. Working on CPU-memory stacking and new memory architectures — "not ready to unfold it." Worth noting: he says memory is no longer the commodity business he used to avoid, which runs against your current stance there.

- The ecosystem edge. ~550 investments, "most connected person" in tech, deep university and VC pipelines. His framing: Intel missed mobile and cloud AI; the plug-in to startups is how he avoids missing the next one.

As a CEO, he is customer obsessed
- Learns in public without embarrassment. Read "CEO for Dummies" cover to cover as a first-time CEO. Told an all-hands to send him ideas, got 300 emails a day, answered every one, then showed up at people's cubicles. His own framing: showing vulnerability makes people want to help you.

- At Cadence he inherited customers so angry they wanted refunds and to stop using the product. Each became an expanding account.

- The old failure mode was ignoring complaints until renewal. He changed it so complaints got fixed inside 24 hours — customers were audibly startled by it.

- Fixing the CPU franchise directly. Admits Intel lost the CPU lead and made "a lot of mistakes" in server. Actively recruiting top CPU, GPU, system and software architects for a full stack — targeting agentic AI, edge, and physical AI, not just PC client.

- Packaging is the option value. EMIB, glass substrates, artificial diamond insulators, microfluidic cooling. He funds startups in these areas personally, then spins them in or acquires them.

- Memory optionality. Hired the ex-SK Hynix head. Working on CPU-memory stacking and new memory architectures — "not ready to unfold it." Worth noting: he says memory is no longer the commodity business he used to avoid, which runs against your current stance there.

- The ecosystem edge. ~550 investments, "most connected person" in tech, deep university and VC pipelines. His framing: Intel missed mobile and cloud AI; the plug-in to startups is how he avoids missing the next one.

As a CEO, he is customer obsessed
- Learns in public without embarrassment. Read "CEO for Dummies" cover to cover as a first-time CEO. Told an all-hands to send him ideas, got 300 emails a day, answered every one, then showed up at people's cubicles. His own framing: showing vulnerability makes people want to help you.

- At Cadence he inherited customers so angry they wanted refunds and to stop using the product. Each became an expanding account.

- The old failure mode was ignoring complaints until renewal. He changed it so complaints got fixed inside 24 hours — customers were audibly startled by it.

- All this still confirms the fact the market is extremely rotationary, and things are still not trending. This is what I wrote to my subs: 

" We continue to be in the phase of "slowing of musical chairs" and you can feel it in the markets - rotations are much quicker, profit being taken. It's a tough environment right now. In times like this I like to have more cash, and just be patient. Remember, cash is a position. That, and zooming out and holding to your core longs."

Frankly, I think the right move is to consolidate into few positions and just hold them. [REDACTED] was a trade that made money. Now I'm going to focus on [REDACTED].

Most importantly though is also knowing what NOT to touch. I feel like semis just don't offer any interesting risk/reward here - memory pumped, then dumped. photonics pumped, then dumped. 

There are no trending assets here - they're good for trades, but goddamn the PA is absolutely brutal and I have no interest in holding anything but [REDACTED] for the long term."

TLDR:
1. You are either a trader that can manage this regime 
2. If you're not, just hold in core positions and wait 

For 2) you also have to make sure your core positions have a future. For example, if your core position is a "high momo" asset that has strong beta but no alpha, you might be cooked for longer than you'd like. You ideally want to hold something that has alpha - something that has a sort of fundamental strength that can be used to justify a long term hold

It's not from Anthropic but from the European Union. The official text is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 which is a sort of GDPR for AI.

"2. Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content, shall ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Providers shall ensure their technical solutions are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as this is technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of various types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. This obligation shall not apply to the extent the AI systems perform an assistive function for standard editing or do not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof, or where authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences."
